Cheap Output, Expensive Judgment
AI burnout, slop mitigation, client-facing effort stratification, and the deskilling that never arrives.
Photo: Lewis Hine, Power house mechanic working on steam pump, 1920. Public domain.
01 · AI BURNOUT
With AI, people work more, not less
53%
More than half of senior engineers now work longer hours than before AI. A year ago it was 28%.
Run fewer agents at once. Count review as real work.
Photo: Switchboard operators, 1958, Seattle Municipal Archives. CC BY 2.0, cropped and toned.
02 · SLOP MITIGATION
Slop is work that looks finished and isn’t
2 hours
What each piece of slop costs the person who receives it: time to check it, fix it or redo it.
If you send it, you must be able to explain it.
Photo: Ford assembly line, Highland Park, 1913. Public domain.
03 · CLIENT-FACING EFFORT STRATIFICATION
Give back the effort you were given
SLOP
Eight pages of generated rambling
Claude writes the reply.
ASK
A real question from a person
A person answers.
RISK
A decision with consequences
Your full attention.
Triage first. Your attention is the scarce resource. “With AI it should be easy” is not a deadline.
Photo: Postal clerks sorting mail, Smithsonian National Postal Museum. No known copyright restrictions.
04 · DESKILLING
No tool has ever removed the need for skilled people
67 vs 50%
Test scores after learning a new library: 67% for engineers who coded by hand, 50% for those who let AI write it.
The job keeps its skill. The person can lose it. Practice without AI.
Photo: Frances Bilas at the ENIAC control panel, U.S. Army, 1946. Public domain.
FOR MONDAY
Output is cheap. Verification is the job.
01
Cap the threads
Limit parallel agents. Count review as work.
02
Gate the slop
The author explains every line. Proof before review.
03
Match the effort
Triage first. Slop gets slop. Attention goes to people.
04
Keep the skill
AI-off practice. Juniors debug by hand first.
